title: Composition versus inheritance (has-a vs is-a)
hook: When you build a service, you usually wire up collaborators instead of extending a giant base class. C# lets you inherit from only one class, so choosing composition early keeps your design flexible.

blocks.text: **Composition** means your type *has* other objects — you store them in fields and call them through interfaces. **Inheritance** means your type *is a* specialized version of a base type — you extend a parent class and reuse its members. In a microservice worker, composition is the default: inject an `IAttemptStore`, an `IBus`, and a `IClock` rather than subclassing `BaseWorker`.

entries.plainDefinition: Building a type by combining other objects (has-a). Dependencies are injected or created inside the type.
Deriving a new class from a base class (is-a). The derived type gets the base's accessible members.
entries.example: `class LtiHandler : AuthHandler` — LtiHandler is a kind of AuthHandler.

entries.plainDefinition: The place in your application where all dependencies are wired together — usually the host or startup code.

blocks.text: Deep inheritance trees couple every derived type to a constructor chain and a protected surface you must keep forever. In production services, that makes versioning painful: changing the base class can break every child. Composition lets you swap implementations — swap Redis for SQL, swap RabbitMQ for an in-memory bus — without touching the worker's class hierarchy. C# reinforces this: you get **one** base class, so wasting it on infrastructure is expensive.

blocks.title: The interview sentence
blocks.body: Say: "I inherit for polymorphism I own; I compose for infrastructure I replace." Then point at a real worker you have shipped, not a textbook diagram.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Ask: is this a genuine is-a relationship?
items.body: If `LtiHandler` truly is an `AuthHandler` with shared validation steps, inheritance may fit. If the worker just needs to call a store, that is has-a — use composition.

items.title: Prefer interfaces for replaceable dependencies
items.body: Declare `IAttemptStore` and `IBus` as constructor parameters. The worker depends on contracts, not concrete types.

items.title: Keep hierarchies small and sealed
items.body: If you do inherit, seal derived types when the set is closed. A sealed `LtiHandler` on an abstract `AuthHandler` is a common production pattern.

items.title: Wire everything at the composition root
items.body: The host registers implementations. The worker never chooses between Redis and SQL — it just calls the interface.

snippet.explanation: Line 1: abstract base shares validation (Template Method). Line 8: `ParseCore` is the variation point. Line 11: `LtiTokenParser` is sealed — no further derivation. The worker composes a `TokenParser`; it does not inherit from one.

snippet.label: Anti-pattern: BaseService dumping ground
snippet.explanation: Line 2: `BaseService` accumulates unrelated concerns. Line 9: `GradingService` is coupled to logging, HTTP, and caching even if it only needs one. Replace with constructor injection of the specific interfaces each service actually uses.

blocks.title: BaseService anti-pattern
blocks.body: A `BaseService` that grows logging, HTTP, caching, and database helpers becomes a dumping ground. Every derived service inherits baggage it does not need. Extract shared behavior into small, focused services or extension methods instead.

blocks.title: Subclassing to tweak one method
blocks.body: If you subclass just to override one method, consider a strategy object or delegate instead. In C#, every subclass consumes your single base-class slot and adds a compatibility promise.

interviewTakeaways: Composition is has-a via constructor injection; inheritance is is-a with one base class.
Microservices stay composition-heavy; class hierarchies stay small and in-process.
Interfaces are how C# adds extra capabilities without a second base class.
commonPitfalls: BaseService that becomes a dumping ground for logging, HTTP, and caching.
Subclassing to tweak one method when a delegate or strategy object would do.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript historically piled behavior on prototypes. Modern JS and TypeScript services compose modules the same way C# workers compose interfaces.
TypeScript mixins fake multiple inheritance. C# uses interfaces plus composition; there is no mixin keyword.
